---
The first thing we lent from the dresser was the drawer itself. A woman named Eileen needed something shallow and reasonably square to carry a cake on two buses. The cake was for her former husband, who had married a diabetic and apparently no longer got what Eileen considered a proper birthday. We lined the drawer with a clean pillowcase. It stuck on the left, and you had to lift it slightly to get it out. I demonstrated this even though, once she had the drawer in her hands, it was information of no conceivable use to her. I was new at the job.

The dresser stood in the lobby of the Marlowe Street baths, which hadn't been baths for thirty years. The city still owned the building and heated it just enough to keep the pipes from bursting. Upstairs there was a rehearsal room, a tax preparation service, and, on Thursdays, a man who repaired accordions. Downstairs there was me. My job title was Building Attendant II. Nobody could identify Building Attendant I. I had a mop, a desk, and a view of the laundromat across the street, where somebody had painted the word WASH backwards on the inside of the window, with the result that it read backwards from outside as well. It takes real conviction to make that particular mistake with an S.

Eileen returned the drawer on Monday. There was a piece of cake in it for me, wrapped in foil, and a square of hardboard cut to fit the bottom. “That wood bows,” she said. “You want to watch that with anything damp.” I thanked her. It was a yellow cake with chocolate icing, the kind I like. She stood at my desk while I ate it, not in expectation of praise, as I first thought, but because she wanted the foil back. It was an unusually good piece of foil, the heavy kind that retains the shape of the thing it has covered. She folded it into quarters and put it in her purse.

By Friday two people had come in asking about the cake carrier. I said what we had was a drawer. One of them said, yes, that was what she meant. She took it to a school supper and brought it back full of teaspoons. She had intended to borrow a few from the supper and had forgotten when to stop. We put the spoons in the top right drawer. By the end of the month the dresser also contained a bicycle pump, a set of pastry cutters shaped like the states of the Union east of the Mississippi, and a pair of binoculars with one working eye. I made a sign: THINGS YOU CAN BORROW. It was meant to distinguish the dresser from my desk. It didn't. My stapler went to a wedding and came back with a pale pink ribbon tied around its middle.

I began keeping records after the bicycle pump disappeared. This was not because I thought keeping records would get it back. We knew exactly where it was. Mr. Diaz had taken it to his brother in Syracuse, experienced a crisis in his marriage, and decided to remain in Syracuse, where he had always been happier. His wife came in especially to tell me this. “Write it down,” she said. “Otherwise whenever you see me you're going to think: bicycle pump.” She was right. Once I wrote it down I was free to think about other things when I saw her, like whether she was doing all right. She was. The brother, it turned out, had a wife of whom she was extremely fond, and they now had long, expensive telephone conversations without either of their husbands interrupting. The pump was ultimately returned by mail at a cost greater than the price of two new pumps.

My records consisted of a composition book with three columns: Object, Name, Expected Back. The third column was the most interesting. Almost nobody could tell you with confidence when they would be finished with a level. They had a shelf to put up, certainly. They had the shelf, the brackets, and the little bag of screws. What they didn't have was any information about the person they would be on Sunday afternoon. Would that person want to put up a shelf? Would that person feel strongly enough about the shelf to move the sofa? Under Expected Back people wrote things like “Sunday unless Ron visits” or “before the baby.” One man, borrowing an extension cord, wrote “when the hedge is beautiful.” He brought it back the next morning. He had quite a small hedge, but he had been right to be ambitious for it.

For a while I became overinterested in the enterprise. I went to yard sales on Saturdays looking for things people might need only once. A melon baller. A pipe wrench. A small, ferocious brush designed to remove pills from sweaters. I spent my own money, not much individually but rather a lot when considered as a sum. These things were almost never borrowed. What people wanted, apparently, were the things other people had already needed and could no longer justify keeping. A plaster foot on which to display a single shoe. A roll of black cloth for photographing an engagement ring you wanted to sell without telling the person who had given it to you. A tape recorder with a button that had to be held down by a thumb or a piece of folded cardboard. People came in for these things with the calm certainty of shoppers who had consulted a catalogue.

“Do you have one of those stools for playing the cello?” a boy asked me one afternoon.

I said I didn't think there was a special stool for playing the cello.

“There is if your feet don't reach the floor.”

We tried him on several chairs. In the end he took the accordion repairman's lunch stool, which had a round seat covered in red vinyl and legs that unscrewed for transport. I left a note for the repairman. The following Thursday he ate his sandwich sitting on the stairs and told me that he preferred it. From the stairs he could see the sky through the high windows above the lobby doors. “I never know what kind of day it is in here,” he said. “All day I hear people letting the air out of things.”

I wish I could tell you I made friends with him. In a story about a public building, two people who spend years under the same roof ought eventually to learn something surprising about each other. But we mostly discussed whether the toilet on the second floor was running again. Once, after a heavy snow, he put a hand on my shoulder to steady himself while he took off his boots. I remember the substantial weight of that hand. I don't remember his first name. I remember the boy because his mother sent me a photograph of him at a recital, sitting very straight on the red stool. Behind him a girl with a violin was looking down into her sleeve, plainly wondering how far up it she could get her hand without attracting the attention of an adult. Quite far, on the evidence.

The trouble began when the city decided the baths were in use. Of course the city had known about us all along. It paid my salary and the gas bill, and once a year a patient woman came to count the fire extinguishers. But in a substantial binder downtown the building had been classified as Underutilized, which meant we were allowed to go about our affairs in peace. Then somebody from the newspaper photographed Eileen carrying the cake drawer down the steps. You could see the painted tiles around the entrance, blue fish blowing blue bubbles, each bubble with a little white crescent to indicate the play of light on water. The photograph ran on a page about neighborhood life. The mayor's deputy recognized the tiles from his childhood swimming lessons. He came to visit with four other people, all of whom had excellent coats. By spring we had been reclassified as a Community Resource.

There followed an interval in which I spent a good deal of time on the telephone explaining the dresser. Was it a tool library? No, although we had tools. Were borrowers members? Of what? Were the items sanitized? I wiped them, if that was what was meant. Could we provide figures for the previous fiscal year? I could, but they would include a woman who had borrowed the same six teaspoons every Wednesday for nine months rather than face the fact that her bridge club was permanent and she needed more spoons. I didn't know if that was one transaction or thirty-nine. The young man on the telephone said it depended on what picture we wanted to paint. I looked across the street. Someone had scraped the W and the A off the laundromat window. For the time being the establishment was called SH, backwards, a request for quiet issued chiefly to people on their way out.

Perhaps you think I'm going to say that the city ruined the dresser. It didn't. The city bought us a handsome steel cabinet with adjustable shelves and a lock that worked. We had needed a lock since a toddler discovered the pastry cutters and tried to swallow Rhode Island. The young man on the telephone turned out to be good at his job. He found a category of municipal property that covered objects recovered from city drains, and under that heading we were able to lend things without requiring proof of residence. He came over on his lunch hour to show me how to fill out the form. He also borrowed a long-handled mirror to see where his cat went when she got behind the refrigerator. He returned it the same afternoon. “There's a whole second cat back there,” he said. He looked tired but pleased, the way people look when a mystery turns out to have been real.

What nearly ruined the dresser was my knee. I had been having trouble with it on the stairs, particularly going down, and then one day I stepped off a curb carrying a grocery bag full of oranges. I didn't fall spectacularly. I sat rather neatly on the curb as if I had decided to wait there for a parade. An orange rolled out of the bag. A man crossing the street changed direction to retrieve it, and for some reason the sight of him changing direction made me understand that I had hurt myself seriously. Before he reached me I was crying hard enough to frighten him. He put the orange in my lap. “I can get the others,” he said, although the others were still in the bag. There are moments when everybody present would be grateful for a straightforward job.

I was gone eleven weeks. The city sent a substitute who knew boilers and had worked in a much bigger building. His name was Len. He found the composition book and did his best with it, but he had the temperament of a man who had kept a large building warm by taking small irregularities seriously. If a person wrote Tuesday in the third column, Len expected to see that person on Tuesday. On Wednesday he telephoned. He did not scold or threaten. He merely said, “We had you down for yesterday,” which proved far more effective. The shelves filled up. The steel cabinet filled up. Things that had been gone so long I had forgotten we possessed them reappeared, including the plaster foot, now wearing a sock someone had knitted to keep it from getting chipped. When I returned, the lobby looked like a shop on the morning before it opens for business, everything arranged and not a soul in sight.

Len had done one thing I would never have thought of. On wet days he put a chair just inside the entrance so people could sit down to close their umbrellas and take off their overshoes. It was the most popular service the building had ever offered. Shoppers stopped to rearrange their bags on it. Children knelt on it to watch for the bus. A courier sat there every afternoon at four to eat a pear. “Nobody borrows anything anymore,” I complained to Eileen. She had come by to inspect my knee, which she regarded as belonging to the neighborhood and having been entrusted, perhaps unwisely, to me. She pointed at the courier. “He's borrowing the chair.” I said that wasn't the same. “Well, don't tell him,” she said. “He's got juice all down his front. He's having a bad enough time.”

The spoons went out again first. Then the level. Somebody took the sweater brush. I kept the record book but stopped asking for dates. Len moved to a new swimming pool out near the airport, where he discovered a faulty valve in his first week and saved the city, according to a letter he sent me, “a not inconsiderable amount of water.” I liked hearing from him. My knee got better up to a point and then decided that point suited it. I kept a cane under the desk. The laundromat hired a sign painter, who put gold letters on the glass, properly facing out. It was called Viola's. In all those years I hadn't known that. I went across one day to see if there was a Viola. There was, and she had been wondering for some time whether we could use a serviceable iron with a very short cord.

Not long before I retired, a young woman came in with the cake drawer. I hadn't seen it in years. One corner had been reinforced with a strip of tin, and the hardboard Eileen had cut was stained in overlapping circles, like a map of islands drawn by someone who had heard about islands but never seen one. The woman set it on my desk. “My grandmother said you'd know where this goes.” For a moment I couldn't think what she meant. Then I went over to the dresser, where we kept the forms now, and pulled out the box of envelopes that occupied the empty space. The drawer went halfway in and stopped. I lifted it slightly. It slid the rest of the way with a soft wooden knock. The young woman asked if that was all. I said yes, and she went out to catch her bus.

All afternoon I kept opening it. I put in the spare pencils, took them out, tried it with the envelopes, decided against them. At five I left it empty and locked up. Across the street Viola was ironing a white shirt in the window, turning the sleeve around the narrow board a little at a time. She raised the iron when she saw me, just an inch or two, cord permitting. I raised my cane. Then she went back to the sleeve, and I went home.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a municipal lending dresser and its narrator’s gradually deepening attention to the people who use it.

## Grounded reading
The voice is wry, observant, and quietly tender, finding meaning in the practical particulars of drawers, foil, teaspoons, and borrowed chairs. Its pathos comes less from dramatic revelations than from small acts of care: recording a neighbor’s circumstances so she won’t be reduced to the bicycle pump, noticing the courier’s bad day, and remembering the weight of the accordion repairman’s hand. The narrator admits the limits of intimacy and memory without turning them into tragedy. The story invites the reader to see a neighborhood as a web of ordinary, sometimes awkward exchanges—and to treat attention itself as a form of kindness.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds useful, worn objects and the uncertain time people need them; municipal bureaucracy and improvised community service; aging and bodily limits; and the modest ties that form between neighbors. Its moral emphasis is that usefulness and care often exceed official categories, while its humor keeps that claim grounded in the peculiar details of daily life.

## Evidence line
> Once I wrote it down I was free to think about other things when I saw her, like whether she was doing all right.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring attention to practical objects, understated humor, and unshowy care gives this story a distinctive, coherent sensibility.
